clue.text: Flashing light set or not, beep occurring intermittently

indicators.note: something that happens intermittently comes and goes, so only every other letter of the words before it counts

parts.note: the first, third, fifth letters and so on of these three words

explanation.surface: Someone describes a flashing light, whether or not it is switched on, with a beep that sounds now and again.
explanation.walkthrough: The odd-numbered letters of 'set or not beep' spell STROBE; the punctuation is only there for the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A strobe is a lamp that emits rapid bright pulses, the kind of flashing lamp used in clubs and photography.

clue.text: When jiggled about, pin set to move!

indicators.note: things jiggled about are shaken around, so the letters land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A bowling pin, once wobbled, is ready to fall over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pin set to move' reads like instructions for a machine; the letters of 'pin set to' make the urging phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Step on it!' is an idiom urging someone to hurry, like 'Get a move on!'.

clue.text: Wobbly old picture

definitions.meaning: first meaning: unsteady, liable to totter
second meaning: the 1976 boxing film starring Sylvester Stallone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Picture' is the old word for a film, and this one is the famous boxing movie.
explanation.definitionFit: Rocky is both an adjective for something unsteady and the title of a classic 1970s motion picture.

clue.text: Baker's mistake?

parts.note: surface reading: an error made by someone baking bread
setter's reading: one word that is both a crusty loaf a baker makes and a slang word for a blunder

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the word for the error is also a kind of loaf.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage a bloomer is a large crusty loaf and also an embarrassing blunder.

clue.text: Paper supply on time

indicators.note: one thing put on another is added to it, so the supply word is tacked on after the time letter

parts.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time
to issue is to supply or hand out

explanation.surface: A notice about paper stock arriving on schedule.
explanation.definitionFit: Tissue is a thin soft paper, used for wrapping or for blowing your nose.

clue.text: Briefly visible through lens, river captured

indicators.note: something captured is held inside its captor, so this letter goes within the phrase

parts.note: anything framed by a camera lens is 'in shot'
R is the standard abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A photographer briefly spots a river through the lens and snaps it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' looks like an abbreviation signal but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: 'In short' is an idiom meaning to sum up concisely, so it equals 'briefly'.

clue.text: Horse fed large alcoholic drink, one of those beaten

indicators.note: an animal that is fed takes something into it, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a steed is a literary word for a horse
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
rum is a spirit made from sugar cane

explanation.surface: A horse is given a big boozy drink, and ends up among the losers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Those beaten' sounds like losers in a race, but it means instruments that are struck.
explanation.definitionFit: A steel drum is a Caribbean percussion instrument played by striking it with sticks, so it is one of those things beaten.

clue.text: Six out of nine go, I stay — one considers no one else

indicators.note: six letters taken out of a longer run of words, left in their order

parts.note: six letters running across these words

explanation.surface: Of nine people, some leave and I remain, thinking only of myself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six out of nine' reads like a count of people; it really says six letters come from 'nine go I stay'.
explanation.definitionFit: An egoist is a self-centred person who puts their own interests before everybody else's.

clue.text: A fool shut in the spinning drier

indicators.note: a thing shut in is enclosed inside something else, so one piece goes within another
spinning sends things whirling round, so the letters of the word it describes get jumbled

parts.note: the letters of the word 'the', spun into a new order
taken as written
a clot is a British informal word for an idiot

explanation.surface: Someone foolish has been locked inside a tumble drier as it spins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spinning drier' suggests a tumble drier, but the definition is a humbler drier: A CLOT goes inside a jumbled THE to make TEA CLOTH.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea cloth is a towel used for drying washed dishes, so it serves as a drier in the kitchen.

clue.text: Fixed, as nails? Quickly too!

parts.note: 'hard as nails' is a common simile, so nails suggest the word for tough
too means also, which is what 'and' adds
fast means quickly

explanation.surface: Something nailed down, and done in a hurry as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard as nails' is a familiar British simile for tough; the clue's question mark warns that nails only hint at the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard and fast describes rules that are fixed and cannot be altered.

clue.text: Copper symbolically said farewell

indicators.note: said means spoken out loud, so we want what the symbol sounds like when voiced

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper; spoken letter by letter it is the answer

explanation.surface: A police officer said goodbye in some symbolic way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a policeman, but it is the metal, whose chemical symbol Cu, read out as two letters, is the parting phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: 'See you' is an everyday parting remark, so it works as a farewell.

clue.text: Politician: choice of extremes for Trotsky?

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two end letters, its very first and very last

parts.note: the opening extreme of the revolutionary's name
'or' is the word that offers a choice between two things
the closing extreme of the revolutionary's name

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a Communist like Trotsky would ever choose a political extreme.
explanation.walkthrough: The extremes of Trotsky are T and Y, and offering a choice between them gives 'T or Y'. Tory is the everyday name for a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A Tory is a Conservative politician in Britain, the opposite pole from Trotsky's Marxism.

clue.text: Superstar finally getting involved, some roles shifted about

indicators.note: letters that are shifted have been moved about into a different order
finally points to the last letter only of the word before it

parts.note: the final letter of the word
taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A star joins a production and the cast list gets rearranged.
explanation.walkthrough: The last letter of Superstar joins the letters of 'some roles' and the whole lot is rearranged. 'About' is the definition at the very end, not part of the shifting.
explanation.definitionFit: 'About' meaning approximately is a synonym for 'more or less', as in 'about ten people came'.

clue.text: PM and Queen talk, in series of minor knocks

parts.note: William Pitt, father and son, were both British Prime Ministers
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the standard abbreviation for the Queen
patter is glib, rapid talk, like a salesman's

explanation.surface: The Prime Minister and the Queen have their weekly chat.
explanation.walkthrough: PM stands for Prime Minister; Pitt the Younger is the crossword's favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitter-patter is the sound of rapid light tapping, such as raindrops or small feet, a run of gentle knocks.

clue.text: Player saw red, one wearing bronze

indicators.note: something being worn is wrapped round the wearer, so these pieces sit inside another

parts.note: a tan is a bronzed skin colour
to see red is to become furious
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A sports player lost his temper while a bronze medallist looked on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' suggests sport, but it is the old theatrical word for an actor.
explanation.definitionFit: A tragedian is an actor who specialises in tragic roles, and a player is an old word for actor.

clue.text: Mythical hero being cool in rising water

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so these letters go within
in a down clue, rising means read from the bottom upward, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: the sea is a body of water
to chill is to cool

explanation.surface: A legendary warrior keeps calm as the water level climbs.
explanation.walkthrough: Achilles fittingly had a link to water: his mother dipped him in the River Styx.
explanation.definitionFit: Achilles is the Greek warrior of Homer's Iliad, a hero of legend.

clue.text: Secondary aim to revise properties of flying objects

indicators.note: to revise something is to rework it, so these letters are reworked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A planner decides to revisit a lesser goal.
explanation.definitionFit: Aerodynamics is the study of how air moves around a body, which governs how aircraft and other flying things behave.

clue.text: Solitary type referring to sign welcoming son

parts.note: re is a short word meaning concerning or about

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so a letter goes inside the word

parts.note: a clue is a sign pointing towards something
S is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A loner mentions a sign that welcomes his son home.
explanation.walkthrough: The irony is that a hermit is welcoming anybody at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A recluse is someone who lives alone and avoids company, a solitary sort of person.

clue.text: Normal insect dropping head on flower

indicators.note: a word dropping its head loses its first letter

parts.note: a gnat is a small biting fly
a flower in crosswords is a river, something that flows; the Ural runs through Russia and Kazakhstan

explanation.surface: An everyday sight: an insect swooping down onto a bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' looks like a bloom but is read as 'flow-er', a river. In a down clue, 'on' puts the first part above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Natural means normal, in keeping with the ordinary course of things.

clue.text: Down perhaps, reckon needing holiday finally

parts.note: to count is to reckon up

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter only of the word before it

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone feeling down reckons they need a holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down' looks like low mood, but it is County Down in Northern Ireland; 'perhaps' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Down is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland, so it is an example of a county.

clue.text: Roman Catholic in small boat off the Sussex coast? Speedy vessel

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so these letters go into the middle of the rest

parts.note: Hove is a seaside town on the Sussex coast in southern England, next to Brighton
a raft is a simple flat boat
RC is the standard abbreviation for Roman Catholic

explanation.surface: A Catholic bobbing about in a little boat just off the south coast of England.
explanation.walkthrough: Hovercraft once ran across the Channel from the Sussex and Kent coast, so the place name fits the scene as well as the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A hovercraft travels fast on a cushion of air over water or land, a quick kind of vessel.

clue.text: Servant forced to dictate?

indicators.note: dictating is speaking words for someone to write down, so we want the spoken form

parts.note: to be forced is to be made to do something; spoken, the word matches a domestic worker

explanation.surface: A servant compelled to take orders, or perhaps to give them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictate' hints at bossing someone about, but here it means saying words out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: A maid is a female domestic servant.

clue.text: So-called fundamental state

indicators.note: so-called points to what a thing is called, a word as people speak it

parts.note: main means chief or fundamental

explanation.surface: A political commentator describes a principle as basic to the nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a verb or a condition, but it is a US state.
explanation.definitionFit: Maine is the northeasternmost state of the USA.

clue.text: New unit is correctly installed

indicators.note: something new is made afresh, so the letters following are made into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A fitter confirms that a new unit has been put in properly.
explanation.definitionFit: In situ is Latin for 'in position', describing something fitted in its proper or original place.

clue.text: Wrong and bad, a Spanish dish

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law
ill means bad, as in ill effects
taken as written

explanation.surface: A diner's verdict: a Spanish dish that is just plain wrong and nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: TORT is the legal term for a wrong done to someone that is not a crime.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish tortilla is a thick omelette with potato, a classic dish of Spain.

clue.text: Twenty to eleven — confirmed the later showing ends there

indicators.note: words showing their ends offer only their final letters to the solver

parts.words: Twenty to eleven — confirmed the later
parts.note: the final letter of each of these six words in turn

explanation.surface: A cinema-goer confirms that the later screening starts at twenty to eleven.
explanation.walkthrough: The time and the screening are all fodder: take the last letter of each word from Twenty through later.
explanation.definitionFit: Yonder is an old-fashioned word for over there, at a distance within sight.

clue.text: Tool sellers dropping drink at the front

indicators.note: dropping something means letting it go, so these letters are taken away

parts.note: suppliers are those who sell goods to others
to sup is to drink, and these are the opening letters to lose

explanation.surface: Hardware sellers spill drinks at the front of the shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Pliers are a gripping hand tool with pincer jaws.
